speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EMPHASIS IN FORTHCOMING SPEECH FROM THE THRONE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is no question that young people are suffering most under the impact of these difficult economic times. Family problems are aggravated by the recession, they are faced with financial problems if they wish to continue their studies, jobs are scarce and when they do manage to get a job, young people are first to be laid off when companies cut back on personnel. At a time when traditional models are being questioned, a time of enormous technological change, a time when serious doubts are being voiced as to the effectiveness of our academic, religious and political institutions, young people are being asked to become part of a society that feels insecure about the future, that jealously guards its past and its vested interests and fails to measure up to the hopes and aspirations of this new generation.
Madam Speaker, I demand that a direct and frank approach be taken to the problems of this new generation. Unfortunately, pressure exercised in a haphazard sort of way has not achieved the expected results, and I would urge the Government to use the throne speech to give the youth issue the emphasis it deserves.
I am very pleased with the step taken by the Government of Quebec this week. It is perhaps not much more than a gesture for the time being, but it is a step in the right direction. I hope that young people in other provinces will also urge their governments to increase their awareness of their concerns, and that our Government will realize at last that the present situation needs more than band-aid solutions and window dressing.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO ABOLISH CHILD TAX EXEMPTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a couple of weeks ago we had the spectacle of the Minister
responsible for the status of women proposing an end to the spousal income tax exemption, and today we are told that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has approved a report recommending that child tax exemptions be abolished.
The Canadian income tax system has always treated the family as a basic unit, and contained the important fundamental concept that a family be able to retain a proportion of its income safe from the tax gatherer's greedy grasp, a proportion needed to sustain the basic necessities of life.
This fair and equitable concept is now under attack by the Liberal Government. There is no telling how far it might go. Presumably the next in line to go will be the exemption for the elderly and pensioners.
Parliament must insist that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) retain the family unit concept within the Income Tax Act and reject out of hand the harebrained schemes of the Minister responsible for the status of women and of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

Madam Speaker, this past week Pope John Paul II's tour of Central America drew world attention to the violence and poverty which afflict that part of the world. Of particular concern to Canadians must be the genocidal war being waged against Indian people by the Guatemalan Government of President Rios Montt.
In the past year thousands of Indian civilians have been killed by the Guatemalan army. Entire villages have been destroyed and hundreds of thousands of Indian people have become refugees, either in their own country or in Mexico. Ail Canadians must join in condemning this brutality, but we must move beyond condemnation.
In addition to an international program of refugee aid, Canada should negotiate with Mexico for international inspection of the deplorable conditions of Guatemalan Indian refugee camps in Mexico.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF QUEBEC MINISTER-ACHIEVEMENTS OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was very pleased to see that the Quebec Government is now taking a more realistic view, according to a statement by a Quebec Minister that was reported in the press. After five years of ignoring the Canadian Government, the Government of Quebec has now realized, and it has said so, that since the Liberals came to power in Ottawa, Quebec had never had so many economic spinoffs, and in his very positive statement, the Minister acknowledged that the federal Members from Quebec were constantly fighting for their province, and he also acknowledged that Bill 101 must be amended to respect the rights of the anglophone community in Quebec and the various ethnic communities that have their own place in our belle province.
Madam Speaker, 1 earnestly hope that the Minister's statement will go beyond mere words and that the Province of Quebec will take action to further the interests of all Quebecers and consequently of all Canadians in this country.

Madam Speaker, yesterday the Minister responsible for the Cape Breton Development Corporation tabled in this House a one and a half inch thick pile of documents which he said related to Devco's involvement in the Scotia Coal Synfuels Project. And what has this shower of paper, that includes 101 pages of academic papers and magazine articles, and 111 pages of requests for proposals and draft legal documents, been meant to accomplish? Obfuscation of the highest order, that is what. A classic cover up is now under way and the Table of this Chamber is being used as a stage for the performance.
How else can one explain the actions of the Devco Minister who, on the pretence of tabling accurate documentation of the Corporation's involvement in the Scotia Coal project, provides not one single piece of correspondence written to its developer? Can you imagine that, Madam Speaker? Devco enters into an industrial consortium with Alastair Gillespie, agrees to invest
up to $300,000 of public money, and never wrote him a single letter. As well, Devco never corresponded once with the Department of Energy, without whose funding the whole scheme would not have materialized in the first place.
It is also hard to believe that since legal counsel for the Energy Department saw fit to write Devco in August, 1981, to request signatures on various documents, no one else ever saw fit to communicate with Devco on the matter previously. Maybe it was Mr. Gillespie who set this pattern of non-letter writing, for of the 315 pages of documents tabled yesterday there is only one piece of correspondence from him to Devco. And this pattern of doing things orally seems to have been picked up within the Corporation as well, for only five internal memoranda are present, four of which are to the president.

subsubtopic: HUNGER STRIKER'S DEMAND FOR PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, on Wednesday, Allan Wilford, the Director of the Canadian Farm Survival Association, was arrested and jailed on a charge related to a penny auction. This penny auction was held to help a young farmer who was losing his equipment to a bailiff, a scene which is becoming all too frequent.
There is a crisis in farm finance spreading across the country that will see many, many more young farmers and their families out on the road. This House must act, and act now, to protect and help these people. We need the food they produce. We need the communities they sustain. We owe them a second chance. We owe them a break until markets turn around or until we can get some decent legislation on the books to improve their incomes.
Allan Wilford is on a hunger strike until this House deals with Bill C-653, an Act to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, or an acceptable substitute. This is a dramatic gesture by a determined young farmer who is leading a group of producers facing the ugly possibility of being refused credit which would enable them to buy and plant their crops this spring.
I urge the Government to relent and give this Bill a chance for speedy passage in the House. We owe it to the farmers of Canada. We owe it to our future.

Noire project at Sept-iles. Considering the problems being experienced on the North Shore at the present time, needless to say there is grave concern in this area, regarding a project that is very important to its development and diversification. Considering the fact that the information was given by management of Iron Ore and that up to now-and I checked this- Iron Ore had never expressed any negative views regarding the development of the Pointe-Noire project, I would like to ask the Minister of Transport who is here in the House (Mr. Pepin) to get in touch with the President of Iron Ore in order to shed some light on the issue, because it is important that the Government be able to take major economic measures so that the North Shore will no longer depend solely on the large multinationals.

Madam Speaker, Patrick Johnston's newly released report entitled "Native Children and The Child Welfare System" demands that renewed attention be given to the plight of native children in our country's child welfare system. It has been clear for some time that, due to a jurisdictional dispute between the Provinces and the federal Government, native children in need of care are left in a legal limbo. Although Indians are the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal Government, child welfare falls within the jurisdiction of the Provinces. Thus, the quality of social services provided to native children varies from Province to Province. The only similarity between the various systems is that everyone agrees that all systems are inadequate and that services provided are well below the level of services provided to non-native children.
Currently the direction being taken by the federal Government seems to be that of encouraging tripartite agreements signed by the federal Government, the Provinces, and Indian organizations in the Provinces involved. Although this serves as a good example to improve the quality of services provided to native children, it avoids resolution of the jurisdictional problem as it pertains to Indian children.
Witnesses appearing before the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government have repeatedly expressed their concern about the inadequacy of the Indian child welfare system. Particularly alarming is the knowledge that Indian children taken into care are rarely placed in Indian homes, thus their cultural ties are irreparably severed. The first step toward rectifying the situation that now exists would be the creation of a federal Indian child welfare act.

speechtext:
Order. When the Committee rose on Thursday, March 10, 1983, Clause 1 was under consideration and the Minister of State for Finance had the floor.
On Clause 1-Value of Benefits

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order concerning the very complex nature of Bill C-139. Researchers have brought to my attention-and I concur with them-that in a legal sense there is incorrect nomenclature in the Bill. It is confusing to begin with, but if the references made therein are wrong, the people who have to translate the passage of the Bill into the Act will not know whether the references are made to the Act or to the Bill. They will have a very difficult time deciphering what has gone on when the Bill passes through the House of Commons.
For example, I refer Hon. Members to page 52, about two-thirds of the way down the page, where Subclause (17) of Clause 12 reads:
Subsection (8) is applicable with respect to transfers occurring after November 12, 1981.
Is that reference to Subsection (8) a Subsection of the Act, which would be the correct nomenclature, or does it really mean Subclause (8) which would refer to the Bill? I would submit that it should actually read Subclause (8), but it does not; it reads "Subsection (8)", which is actually a reference to the Act itself. Am I correct in that understanding? If so, I would point out that there is an inconsistency throughout the Bill.
Next I draw the attention of Hon. Members to page 47 of Bill C-139, again about two-thirds of the way down the page, where adjacent to "(6)" there is a reference made to Subsection 20(8) of the said Act. Then on page 48 there is a reference under Subclause (8) to Subsection 20(14) of the said Act.
Returning to the item on page 52 to which I drew Hon. Members' attention, it either refers to Subclause (8) of Clause 12 of the Bill or Subsection (8) of Section 20 of the Income Tax Act. Therefore, it becomes very unclear what the Bill refers to when it uses the word "Subsection". The Bill seems to be littered with a number of apparent inconsistencies.
If Hon. Members will direct their attention to page 52a, the bottom line thereof, they will see a reference wherein the Subsection and Subclause are clearly distinguished, as substantiated by the reference to Subclause (4) of Clause 11 of the Bill. This would refer us back to page 37 where we find Clause 11(4), which reads:
Section 18 of the said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after subsection (3) thereof, the following subsections:
The Bill goes on from there. I am concerned with the word "Subclause." It should be used consistently with reference to a Bill of this House.

You are right.
March 11, 1983

The word "Subsection" should refer explicitly to the Income Tax Act. There are many inconsistencies throughout Bill C-139 which make it very confusing whether the reference is to the Bill or to the Income Tax Act, not only for Members of the House, but also for those who have to translate the information once the Bill passes through the House.
If I am correct in the observations I have made, what are we going to do to clear up this very apparent inconsistency in Bill C-139?

Mr. Chairman, I understand that we are continuing consideration of Clause 1 of the Bill before us. We have dealt with a number of Sections, none of which it seems to me were referenced by the Hon. Member who has just spoken. He did begin by making reference to Clause 17. My submission to the Chair and to Hon. Members is that we really cannot, under the pretext of one Hon. Member's interpretation of the Section, move from one Section to another. For example, the Hon. Member indicated the problem was interpersed throughout the Bill. The only way in which we can deal with this item is to deal with it in the context of the matter before Hon. Members. If the matter affects Clause 1, which we are in the middle of considering, that is the only reasonable way we can attempt to come to grips with the objections, suggestions or interpretations of Hon. Members on any aspect of the Bill. Otherwise, it would become hopeless to cope with.
On the thrust of the argument made by the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake, I would appreciate having the observations in writing. I am told the Department of Justice has recommended a different way of numbering and a different way to describe. It is new, but that is recent advice from the Department. I would like the opportunity of giving the Hon. Member the Department's view on that. However, I think it ought not to interfere with the regular business of this Committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wonder if the Chair could observe that the Bill is drafted with reference to legislation, in which case the references are in terms of Sections. For purposes of consideration in the House, we refer to Clauses. Is this the source of confusion for the Hon. Member?

No, Mr. Chairman, that is not the source of confusion. I disagree with the Minister, with all due respect, but I believe we should get this problem clarified and cleared up before we proceed with this Bill because it could very well be wasted time. In some cases within Bill C-139, references are made in the Bill to delete or go back to a Subsection. Since the word "Subsection" is used throughout Bill C-139 instead of "Subclause", it is very confusing whether or not the references are to the Bill itself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would draw the Hon. Member's attention to the fact that the draft before us relates to existing Statutes. It is a practice of the House to refer to Statutes by Section, whereas with consideration by the House, the practice is to
Income Tax
refer to Clauses. It appears that is the point which the Hon. Member has not fundamentally grasped.

Mr. Chairman, I think the Hon. Member may well have a point but it is a very confusing one. He has gone through a number of pages and mentioned a number of Sections. Member is speaking in Clause 1. Therefore, we could proceed with Clause 1. I think, though, that what the Hon. Member has raised is important, and if in fact what he has raised is the case, then it could be that a good many parts of this Bill are incomprehensible to everyone, including people in the legal drafting business, and obviously the House cannot deal with it.

We all know that the Income Tax Act is incomprehensible anyway, but if it is so incomprehensible that it cannot be put together in an Act that some persons can read, then the incomprehensibility goes beyond the ability of the House to deal with it. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake raises as concerns are within the ambit of Clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, I could agree to that and will not unduly delay the business of the House any longer if you can provide me with the assurance that at the next sitting of the Committee of the Whole dealing with Bill C-139 we will, in fact, deal with this problem that I have brought up today. If I can have the assurance of the House and the Chairman that we will do that, I will not delay the discussions any longer.

Member. When we come to the first Section in which it would be pertinent, if we are still not in agreement I think that would be the appropriate time to deal with it.

Therefore, if he has a Cadillac and his neighbour, another chauffeur, has a Toyota, in both cases they decide for themselves, as reasonable adults, whether they will take advantage of their cars for personal use. Mr. Chairman, can the Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary explain to the House how, on January
1 of any given year, I am to know exactly what the maintenance costs will be on my vehicle over the 12 months ahead in order to make this intelligent decision?

speechtext:

Member has paid for the personal use of his car in after-tax dollars, so we are asking people with company-supplied cars to pay for personal use in after-tax dollars. That is all.

Equally, if a salesman wants to use a company-owned car for personal use, then that salesman pays for the personal use in after-tax dollars. There is nothing more uncomplicated or fair than that. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is the same answer. It is the taxpayer's personal choice to drive those 12,000 kilometres. If the taxpayer chooses to do so, then the taxpayer derives a personal benefit and pays tax on it. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Agreed. Accordingly, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South is in good order and the Chair finds his proposed amendment to be acceptable procedurally; so we can carry on debate in that regard.

Mr. Chairman, the effect of the amendment is to adopt the same type of attitude which was taken in the Senate Committee studying the proposed provisions of the Income Tax Act. The Senate in its wisdom felt that when the standby charge related to the value of an automobile, it should not relate to the original cost but to the cost as it goes down, is altered or changed over the life of the vehicle. The effect of our amendment would be to provide, if the car was worth only $2,500, a standby charge of 2 per cent of that amount per month. If it was worth $5,000, it would be 2 per cent of that amount per month, and so on.
There is no reason, in the concept of fairness, why the standby charge should remain constant through the life of the vehicle when the value of the vehicle to the owner, the value to the employer and indeed the value of the vehicle on the market, has gone down and down and down. We could have the terrible situation that if a company was not doing too well and could not afford to replace its salesman's car, the salesman would be driving around in an older, progressively rustier, beat-up car but would be stuck paying the same standby charge as was paid when the car was brand-new. That is a disgraceful situation in terms of fairness. If the whole question of the taxation of standby charges is to be fair to the people of Canada, then surely it should be fair in relation to the progressively lesser value of the car as it gets older.
Why does the Minister think that the proposal in the Bill at present is fair and the amendment should not be carried? In any sense of fairness the amendment makes sense.

Mr. Chairman, as I indicated, the question of valuation is a difficult one especially when dealing with motor vehicles. I submit in seriousness to all Members that motor vehicles are of different value, work better at different times
Income Tax
and follow no average or common pattern in so far as performance is concerned, even when two vehicles come off the assembly line one after another.
For that reason the proposal of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South was not adopted by the Government. I say this notwithstanding the fact that we have submissions from the Senate Committee. Mind you, that recommendation was not paralleled in the recommendation of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. We think that in fairness to Canadian motorists and those people who are affected by, and want to take advantage of, the use of vehicles for personal reasons while in the employment of companies offering these benefits, rather than a year-by-year valuation we should take the average valuation for the vehicle over its life.
What the Hon. Member is doing in this amendment, as he has done in every amendment he placed before us, is to invite greater complexity and paper work. This offends the very thing for which they criticize the Government, that is, for not properly administering the application of this Section.
Could we imagine the situation if every taxpayer, every driver of automobiles, had in addition to keeping track of their mileage to put a year-by-year valuation on their vehicles, taking into account all of the matters affecting it?
No problem.
I hear the Hon. Member saying "no problem".
The Blue Book tells us the value every year.

He is blowing hot and cold. On the one hand he tells us that the Section as it is now is too complicated and too difficult for taxpayers to understand or manage. Yet he invites us to go through what is the most complicated and variable process of all valuation processes, that is, to put a valuation on a used motor vehicle.
I know the Hon. Member is a practising solicitor and that he has had experience in the settlement of motor vehicle claims. He knows the difficulties surrounding the valuation of motor vehicles in such suits. He knows that it is virtually impossible on a unit-by-unit or vehicle-by-vehicle basis to arrive at a valuation which is agreeable to any two people.
That is just absolute nonsense.
The Section as it is takes the average value and breaks it down over the life of the vehicle.
No, it does not.

It is not taken year by year. If the Hon. Member were really serious in his proposal and expected to achieve the same revenues under the Section, I presume he would have no quarrel with the amount of revenue expected from the first year the standby charge would be in effect. We would probably have to increase the charge from 2 per cent to something higher, because 2 per cent is based upon the value

March 11, 1983
Income Tax
of the vehicle, not the average value. As he indicated, in the first year there may not be the expenses which there may be in the fifth year.
Therefore, he would not only have to amend the Clauses which he referred to in order to achieve the desirable revenues, which his Party has indicated is acceptable in principle, but he would have to make further amendments to the Clause. In effect, what he is proposing is an administrative monstrosity. It would be an imposition upon the owner of a vehicle who would have to come up with that valuation, demonstrate it and prove it to the officials of National Revenue as he prepared his returns each year.

The amendment as filed does not refer to fair market value. It refers to the undepreciated capital cost of the vehicle. If the Minister knows anything about the way people carry automobiles on their books, he should realize that the cost is the undepreciated capital cost. What we want is to have the depreciation, as it goes on on a capital cost basis every year, be the cost on which the standby charge is calculated. It is very simple because the capital cost of the vehicle must be determined by every employer every year in the normal course of business. We are not putting the employer through any additional work. We are not complicating the matter. All we are doing is bringing some fairness into the situation.
With respect to the Minister's statement concerning the complications of this Act, he is quite right. If we had our way, we would throw most of it out for that reason. But unfortunately, the House and the people of Canada will be stuck with this Act. If you have to be stuck with it, you might as well have a little fairness brought into it. The way it is now it is totally unfair.
This whole proposal was brought to the people of Canada on the basis of increasing fairness, yet the Minister wants to be unfair. He even wants to be so unfair as to say there are revenue considerations and, therefore, he would have to increase the standby charge because he has to get all the revenue he can. He is not interested in fairness. He is interested in taxing people, employers and employees who happen to have company cars. That is what he wants to do.
What we want to do is to bring some fairness to this Section. We are saying to the Minister that the standby charge should be calculated on the basis of the capital cost of the vehicle on an annual basis to the employer. That is all. In other words, you should not pay a standby charge higher than the cost of the vehicle to the employer. That strikes me as eminently fair. But the Minister goes on to say that you cannot figure out the cost and the value of the vehicles. Presumably people could cheat. Is it not very easy to do that?
In Toronto the Minister knows that there are Blue Book values of almost every car produced anywhere in the world. The Minister knows that car values are determined all the time. He knows that provincial Governments collect the sales taxes and if someone tries to claim a car at less than fair market value originally, or less than its value as it depreciates.
and it is sold as a used car to try to avoid payment of tax based on value, then it is not very long before a revenue officer is around to collect the correct amount of tax. Therefore, the arguments put by the Minister are nonsense.
The Minister then referred to the standing committee that examined the matter. Let us talk about that and let me read from the standing committee's report. On page 8 of this report, we find:
Some have suggested that the proposed imputed benefit seemed high considering that almost the full value of the company-owned car is imputed to the user over four years. This observation overlooks the higher repair and maintenance costs that are covered by the standby charge and which generally increase with the age of the car.
That statement is in the committee report because when the committee went over the previous Ways and Means motion, the use benefit-in other words, the cost of operating the vehicle-was not to be included as a cost to the employee. But the Department in its desire to up taxes decided not to charge the employee the standby charge. The Department decided to do one thing further and add in the maintenance cost of the car attributable to personal use. In other words, the Department dramatically increased the burden on employees using company-owned vehicles. The standing committee looked at the matter. That is the reason the standing committee did not come up with the firm direction to have some sort of amortization of capital cost in determining standby charges.
The very purpose of that objection to Clause 1, when the standing committee considered this matter of maintenance costs, repair costs, licence fees, insurance costs, was that these costs were not to be attributed to employees. Now they are to be attributed to employees. That is why the standby charge should be organized in relation to the value of the vehicle and not to the original invoice purchase price.

Mr. Chairman, I can only assume that when the Hon. Member referred to capital cost as being the basis for the calculation of the charge, he really meant undepreciated capital cost. That is the basis of the unamended Section. I think he meant undepreciated capital cost.
I make reference to that because the minority view of the Hon. Member, as a member of the standing committee, was not reflected in a recommendation to the Government, no doubt in part because his amendment and his view was not well thought out. The basis for his argument is that the value should be on undepreciated capital cost. That provision in the Act is a concept which applies only in certain circumstances. It would not apply as a general rule across the whole spectrum of people who conceivably would be subject to the tax, as has been the case since 1971 and is being amended.
The Hon. Member, who is attempting to assist the Government with his amendment to come up with what he perceives to be a fair method for taxation, really has proposed a way that will not work and is defective. What about the fleet situation? Firms, even though they have fleets, conceivably may not be taking capital cost allowance. It is an interesting idea but it is one that is only a partial formula and is grossly
March 11, 1983

unfair to those people who cannot take advantage of fleets. The small-businessman, for instance.
We know that the majority of people who are affected by this provision do not take advantage-
They do.

The Hon. Member, with respect, has an interesting thought. It was rejected by the committee, and the Government, of course, for the reasons I have given, could not accept it. It is a defective formula. It is an unjust formula. It is a most unfair and inequitable proposal for a formula.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few questions for the Minister on which I need some clarification. I think what has annoyed most of the people involved with a leased vehicle is that the lease is already in effect and they have no way of backdating it or making an adjustment to it. In effect, what the Government is doing with this provision in Bill C-139 is reaching back to 1982 and placing an additional tax on the individual who is using the vehicle.
I think that is the key point of the whole debate. The Minister is reaching back a year into 1982's income and saying that the Government will impose an extra tax on an individual by reason of this provision in Bill C-139. That is the nub of the whole issue.
A number of people who have corresponded with me have proposed that the implementation of this tax be delayed until the 1983 taxation year in order to allow those who have committed themselves to a lease to make an adjustment. That is one of the matters that I would like to comment on. Why can this not be done with some more reason, and in this particular case dealing with personal use of vehicles, make the change effective in the taxation year 1983?
I think that would cause the whole matter to move more expeditiously. It would then appear to those involved that there is some justice. People can then make the adjustment to their income with their employer or make whatever other adjustments they wish in the handling of the automobile if this was implemented for the taxation year 1983. Has the Minister considered that? If we move an amendment to that effect, would he look upon it favourably?
Income Tax

Mr. Chairman, indeed, we have considered that request because it is one that has been made by a number of individuals and representatives of various trade organizations that have been interested in this Clause.
I would have to remind the Hon. Member for Burlington that this provision in the Act is one that has been in place since 1971. It does not come as a surprise to fleet owners or anyone else who has been affected by the charge. Indeed, business people have been conducting their affairs under this tax provision for a number of years; it does not come out of the blue. The proposed amendment is to change the rate of tax that is levied.
I gave the rationale for the Government moving to change that rate in 1981, bearing in mind the costs and other changes in the economy since 1971.
I would further point out that this is not a retroactive proposal by the Government. This was a proposal introduced in November of 1981 which was to be effective in 1982. Therefore, rather than retroactive, it is prospective.
With respect to a delay until 1983, I do understand the representations that have been made about forgetting 1982 and beginning to talk about this measure for 1983. I am told by officials, however, that two separate publications were made available by Revenue Canada in their supplement to the 1981 employers and trustees guide as well as a special release through an interpretation bulletin IT-470 which was issued early in 1982 and which brought these changes to the attention of the business community in the normal course that has been followed for the last 10 years.
Although we are sympathetic to those people who would obviously like some time to rearrange their business decisions and their budgets-of course, they would like another year to prepare for that-the Government, however, has adopted the position that the announcement of the intention to change two months before it was to happen, which was in late 1981, was adequate notice for people to conduct their affairs in 1982. I have been told by a number of chartered accountant firms that most people have in fact done that. It was not particularly complicated. It was merely a matter of changing the amounts in a practice that they had already been carrying out under the 1971 law.

of which he has calculated his private mileage to be 1,660 kilometres. He said: "Based on this calculation, it is costing me 46 cents a kilometre for the private use of this car".

I maintain that the 1 per cent, the way in which the Government did it in the first place, was unfair. That is the point. It was unfair because it was not based on the undepreciated value. Possibly we did not raise it at that time. We probably did but no one listened, as is usually the case. I maintain that the person pays $2,400 in the fourth year but he still has $1,000 or perhaps $3,000 worth of repairs, whereas in the first year he pays $2,400 and has maybe $200 in repairs. This is inequitable.
If the Government wants corporations to get rid of their cars, that is fine. The Minister made another statement, that small businesses do not benefit. If they do not benefit by the second tax year, they are in financial trouble, but they have
March 11, 1983

not paid taxes because they can write it off. Many of them, as a result of the lower tax rate for small business, benefit greatly by bringing a 50 per cent rate down to a 20 per cent rate because of these write-offs.
I think the Government has to deal with this, not just pass over it. The constituency out there is somewhat annoyed. People are hurting. How much does the Government want to hurt Canadians? Does it want to remove itself from power forever? Surely it should look to the future and do something to help the people who supported it in the past.
There are options available. There is the Blue Book value or the depreciated value; the Government must take one or the other, not a straight line. Another alternative would be to take the average cost of repairs in the first year, and anything in excess of that amount could be deducted from the capital cost after the first year. That would be another way of getting around it. I am just saying that it is inequitable and, if the Government made some adjustment in this regard, it would be fair. I would like to know what the Government is considering because I know it is stonewalling us on it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to remind the Hon. Member that no one who purchases a car for personal use can apply the calculations he is talking about. Therefore, when we ask about personal use company-owned cars, we simply ask that people have the same rules and the same treatment. That is all we are saying. If the Hon. Member wants to come up with a sliding scale of values that reflect the resale value of the car, perhaps the Hon. Member could explain how he would apply that same sliding scale to private purchases so that people could get equal benefit on private automobiles rather than company automobiles. All we are asking for is the same treatment for the same use.
How about putting it together again?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If we take an example of a car with a lease value of $300 a month and add perhaps another $100 a month for operating costs, then we are probably looking at $3,600 added on to an individual's taxable income in a year. If that individual is at the 50 per cent tax bracket, then he would pay $1,800 tax to get a car, pay for his gas, insurance, repairs and everything else. I do not know how many people have a personal car that only costs them $1,800 a year. There are not very many. Under the existing law, which we are amending, that same car would only be worth $1,200 in a taxable benefit which, at a 50 per cent rate, would result in a $600 bill. Even at $1,800 the car is the cheapest car on the block. You cannot get a cheaper car than that.
How about year four?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We are talking about a $300 a month leased car that is operated and worth only $1,800 to the individual in the highest tax bracket.
Income Tax
What about a person with a 33 per cent tax rate? Let us add on this $3,600 benefit. It costs the individual $1,200 a year to drive a car, pay for his gas, insurance, and maintenance. That is a pretty cheap car. I think the Hon. Member should put the numbers down in black and white before talking about inequity. It is not inequitable. The very proposal he is recommending is inequitable because of the complexity and the paper work involved, which would be enormous. I would remind the Hon. Member that a spokesman for his Party in the House of Commons yesterday, as reported in Hansard at page 23668, said:
The Progressive Conservative Party position is as follows: While the principle of taxing this benefit is not unacceptable, the rate of taxation and the method of calculation is suspect. The negative impact of the tax increase overshadows the benefits of increased revenues. It should be amended downward. The sections of the Act dealing with calculation of benefits should be clarified along with the regulations.
That is exactly what we are talking about.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I want to contrast that lofty sentiment with the figures. The figures I just gave indicate that a taxpayer in the highest tax bracket, after the passage of this measure would pay $1,800 a year for gas, insurance, maintenance and the vehicle. That is pretty cheap. If Hon. Members want that geared down, Mr. Chairman, maybe they would like us to give a free car to everyone instead of taxing them.
Mr. Chairman, I would rather not hear that. That may be another one of the Liberals' give-away programs. We cannot afford what the Liberals have done already.
That is what you are recommending.

No, I am not. I am recommending fairness and equity. Your explanation in the first year is fair. But as a private individual driving a car, which I am now, because I do not get an allowance for using a car around here, I am much better off to own my car rather than take 2 per cent on the capital cost. To me, the price is unfair. If it were on a graduated scale, it would be equitable, but the Government's formula is inequitable. It is unfair. Let me give one other argument.
We do not have enough salesmen in this country. We do not have enough people pushing Canadian products. As a result, we are dependent upon imported products. We should give salesmen encouragement, rather than discouragement. I think salesmen are a very important segment of our society. I say they are being unfairly treated.
I believe in equity and fairness. I do not disagree with the Minister for the first year. I heard the Minister say the Government was going to put it up to 3.5 per cent.
That is your amendment.

The Liberals are always finding new ways to grab new bucks. That is the name of their game. You look everywhere for bucks. That is the game it plays. The National Energy Program is a prime example. It did not work. It is going to blow your brains out. With respect to the subject
23714

March 11, 1983
Income Tax
under discussion, I say to the Minister, do not let this come back to haunt you the way the National Energy Program will.
I hear the Minister's comments. While the Liberals are in power, they can say whatever they want. But I am talking about constituents, those people who elected you who may think twice the next time.
Two per cent is better than 3.5 per cent.

I am talking about equity. I am saying that in the first year it is fair. I hear the Minister again. You are skimming funds right off the top. You have a way of skimming money from the public. You will take it any way you can, and then you pay off people to the tune of $1 million like Gillespie did to set up a plant that was not going to be worthwhile in the first place.
Let us be realistic. If the Government looks after its expenditures, it can look after its income. Because expenditures are out of control, the Government cannot look after its income. I say, be equitable. The first year, fair ball. I agree. The second year, a depreciated value, including repairs. I agree with that totally. The third year, another one-third off and the repairs. I agree with that.
There goes S20 million.

It is not $20 million. If you can show me the figures that show it kisses $20 million goodbye, I will accept them, but I will analyze them very carefully. The Government is cutting its own throat by putting this Bill through. Salesmen have written to the Minister. I hope he has read their letters. I have answered all of their letters even though they were not addressed to me, because I am concerned about them. The Government almost put the life insurance people out of business. They lobbied so hard the Government had to retract much of the law. You have not listened to the salesmen of this country, and I think you should.
I plead with the Minister to consider allowing a fair amount in depreciation each year so that the salesman is not paying the same amount for capital costs in the fourth year as he is in the third year. I am delighted to see one of the Minister's own colleagues agreeing with me on this point. Even the Minister's own people agree with me.
Hear, hear!

It is fair. These people need that help. They are not selling as many products. They are not producing as much income, and now the Government is going to tax retroactively that much harder. I ask the Minister to consider this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a brief comment on the statement just made which was so eloquently and passionately expressed. If I ever go back into sales, I will certainly be looking up the Hon. Member. He is a real spokesman.
On the other hand, I would like him to follow the example I gave him. I indicated to him that a car with a leased value of $300 a month which costs $100 more for gas, oil and all the
rest, would total $3,600 in the first year. At a 50 per cent bracket, the individual would pay $1,800. He said that was fair. I would like him to follow that example through. Over four years there is an expense to the taxpayer in after-tax dollars of $7,200. That is a four-year expense for leasing and operating that vehicle. A vehicle held on a $300 a month lease is a $10,000 vehicle.
If his neighbour were to purchase the same vehicle, he would have a $10,000 vehicle.
He is better off.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The Hon. Member says that he is better off, but he is not. He is $10,000 in the hole, whereas the taxpayer we are talking about is only $7,200 in the hole. Of course, the difference is that when the vehicle is traded in, he will hopefully be given a $3,000 trade-in after four years.
I would ask the Hon. Member again to go back to the data and not just make impassioned speeches, because his speeches are really hiding the fact that the standby charge that we have here reflects current values. It does not, as he says, distort the values over the years.
Just one point, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I appreciate the Hon. Member's desire to speak but I must indicate to him that his time has expired and I should move on to another Hon. Member. He may wish to seek unanimous consent of the House to make his comment. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

There is just one thing to keep in mind. When a salesman drives a car, the car is driven more miles and receives far greater wear and tear. The Hon. Member knows that as well as I that the cost of maintaining the car in the fourth year is much higher.
Perhaps the way for the salesman to get around this is to lease a car for one year, lease it at a lower rate at the end of the first year and lease it again in the third year at a lower rate. Perhaps there is a way around the law, but that still does not acomplish what he is dealing with. I hope the Government does not change the law because I brought this up.
Whenever a law is made, people will think of ways to get around it. I would recommend to my constituents that that is what they do. I would tell my local dealer to lease the car for one year, lease it the second year at a reduced amount and again in the third year at a reduced amount. Avis and Tilden do it that way, and perhaps they will get all the business and leave the other leasing companies with none.
I wanted to raise that point, particularly about the fact the amount of miles that a salesman puts on his car is much harder on a car than family use.
March 11, 1983

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the obvious corollary to that, in the case of a salesman using his vehicle, is that he should not use it for personal use.

Mr. Chairman, I want to pursue that with the Parliamentary Secretary. I want to ask him about the question of equity between owning and leasing, because that is clearly a business decision. I think the Parliamentary Secretary would accept that.
Let us use the example given by the Hon. Member for considering the value of buying and operating a car versus leasing a car. Suppose that a person owns and operates a car for six years for which the standby charge will be the same every year. Suppose a person leased the same kind of car, with the same operating costs, the same mileage and personal usage factors, for the normal period of three years, and then leased it again at a lower rate. The result will be that the salesman who drives the company-owned car is charged, based on the ownership standby, the same amount for every year for six years, whereas in the alternative, the company that leases the car which has the same mileage and operating costs will have its tax effect fall in the last three years on a renewed lease.
In other words, leasing will allow people to benefit from the amendment. This can be extended to the previous Member's comments, because leasing can be done annually or semiannually. Why is it wrong to allow people who choose to own the car to benefit from the amendment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as our official indicates, it is an interesting example, particularly because most leases are for two years, not six years. However, there are such things as six-year leases.
I think it bears some examination. The equal principle here, which I appreciate the chance to state now, is that such arrangements are the private matter of the taxpayer. They are not matters into which we want to intrude. If a taxpayer decides to lease instead of purchase, or decides to own an expensive car instead of a cheap one, that is the taxpayer's concern and not ours.
I urge the Hon. Member to read some of the debate on the issue in 1971. I remember very clearly that all of these types of issues were raised at that time. People said over and over again, as did the Hon. Member for Ontario a few minutes ago, that salesmen would stop using company cars and that we would see exotic dodges on the tax law and we would see different methods used. That did not happen.
All that has happened is that the standby charge has become dated as the automobiles have increased in value. In effect, we are updating the standby charges to reflect the market value of the vehicles.

Mr. Chairman, that is mythical. That is the theory which says that as values rise, tax rates should rise. That has to be one of the greater nonsenses expressed in the House.
The Parliamentary Secretary is saying that there should be a bias in the tax system. The Minister is now making the same assertion that there should be a bias in the system in order to
Income Tax
save tax by leasing. The effect of that bias in the tax system means that those who finance vehicles should make more money than those who buy them. That is the effect of allowing an individual to achieve a reduction in the taxable benefit through leasing annually. I find it unbelievable that the Government does not realize that.
My question is with respect to leases themselves. It is a question asked by a constituent for which 1 do not have the answer. If I trade in an automobile worth $4,000 and take a new car on a lease, as opposed to buying it, let us say that it would cost $350 a month to lease the car. Therefore, I presumably would owe the charge on $350. If I trade in my old car and its credited value reduces the lease cost to $250 per month, will I be charged tax on $350 or $250?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This is indeed a technical question and one that we can verify for the Hon. Member. I take it that it is a question from his constituent, and I will ask our officials to give him an answer as quickly as possible.
I would remind him, however, that whatever answer is forthcoming it is based on 12 years of experience. It is not one that will come as a result of this law. This law does nothing but change the rate, and the Member is asking us about an established tax practice. We will give him the technical answer to that question. I understand the intention of what he is asking, and we will make sure that he gets a reply.

Mr. Chairman, it relates specifically to this amendment. I suspect that the answer to the question in my example is $250. Therefore, I suspect that there continues to be a bias toward leasing. If I am in a situation where my $10,000 automobile, which is now worth $4,000, will cost me as though it were worth $10,000 for tax purposes, it is worthwhile for me to trade it in with its $4,000 value and lease either a new or a used car and lower the cost on which tax is charged. Therefore, it is important to the amendment and goes back to my belief, from what I have read, that the Government's practice is to push people toward leasing as opposed to owning. That is a principle to which I do not subscribe.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I take it that the Hon. Member feels that the law, as it exists now, is biased toward people who lease. He believes that the increase in the rate will increase that bias. Our officials have not found that to be the case.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to pursue the matter, because I was interested in the debate between the Hon. Member for Calgary West and the Parliamentary Secretary with regard to this issue. I do not want to be taken the wrong way, because I know the Parliamentary Secretary did not like the range of questions. However, this is the question: if I, as an ordinary Canadian, take my children to a movie on Saturday night in a company automobile, that is considered to be personal use of the automobile. Is that correct? The Parliamentary Secretary is shaking his head. If the Prime Minister of Canada takes his children to a movie on

March 11, 1983
Income Tax
Saturday night and is required, for the safety of the office and the person of the Prime Minister-
Or the Leader of the Official Opposition.
-to have this security-it is a very simple question, Mr. Minister. There is no reason to interject. It could be the Leader of the Official Opposition.
Then stop fooling around and stop using the Prime Minister as an example.
I would not use the Prime Minister as an example of anything for any Canadian.
Then what are you doing, and why are you asking the question?
I am asking a question about the law.
You are being political and wasting the time of the House.

Some Liberals might pay attention to questions about the law. I know Liberals do not like the law. It interferes with their habits.
My question is this simple one: if a Cabinet Minister takes his children, or if the Leader of the Opposition takes his children-
His child.

-to a movie on Saturday night and security is required, is it any less a personal use of the automobile? If it is no less a personal use of the automobile, will personages in that situation, whether they be the Leader of the Opposition, a Cabinet Minister, a Premier of a Province or the Prime Minister of Canada, be required to pay personal tax on the use of that car for that evening?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will certainly investigate to determine the basis for this one standard concerning security personnel, and will try to answer the question for the Hon. Member. I do believe, as he said himself, that the issue is a bit distorted. I only ask him to remember that this is one of several guidelines in the Treasury Board bulletin to Ministers which indicates the difference between personal and public or business use of a vehicle. Bell Canada, Ontario Hydro, General Motors and all other large organizations have similar manuals for their employees. I am sure that there are also standards in those manuals which give rise to questions of equity like this one.
I would think that after some scrutiny, with the reasonable amount of experience we have had over the past 12 years, we will find that these guidelines are explainable and acceptable. We are dealing with a body of experience, and every large organization will try to give to its employees the benefit of such experience in the form of guidelines. The guidelines will then dictate the dividing line within that organization between personal and public use or personal and business use. I think it is reasonable to have guidelines. That is all we are reflecting upon here. If the Hon. Member wants a technical answer on
the use of one guideline out of many to define the difference between public and private, then we will provide him with that explanation. That is a reasonable question and we will provide it to him.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The Hon. Member for Don Valley West, just before the Parliamentary Secretary commenced his reply, commented to the effect that Hon. Members on this side did not respect the law or found the law to be inconvenient. I am sure that, upon reflection, he will want to withdraw those remarks. Even though it is 4.15 p.m. on a Friday, it is surely not in keeping with the character of this House to trade personal abuse across the floor, especially the allegation of illegalities or illegal conduct. I take very strong personal exception to those comments. If the Hon. Member wants to stick around this particular institution for a long period of time, he will surely respect the institution and the Hon. Members within it.

Mr. Chairman, 1 hope that you, the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary will carefully listen to my remarks. Much time has been spent on interventions with regard to Clause 1. I know that the questions which have been raised are very pressing to a certain group of people. I think they have been more than adequately covered with regard to Clause 1. In my own situation, I suspect that less than 1 per cent of the people in my entire constituency would be affected by the Clause. The concerns of any who would be affected have already been covered in the interventions I have heard.
The questions which I pose to the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary are connected to Clause 1 in that if the Bill does not soon pass, there will be many people who will be inconvenienced because income tax returns will have been filed and duly processed by the Revenue Canada taxation branch as best it can, but I understand it does not have the authority to issue cheques to these people. Some two million income tax forms have been processed by Revenue Canada and placed in the computer. Once Bill C-139 is passed, it will only be necessary to punch a button and the cheques will be issued through the computer system-
Do it right now. It will do it.

-to people who are eligible for income tax refunds. The people of Revenue Canada do not feel they have the authority to do that. They have done a very good job in processing the applications they have received. However, if there were some change to the parliamentary and democratic process of the House as a result of Bill C-139, it could cause some horrendous problems for them in terms of recalling payments or making adjustments to some of the cheques which had been sent out to people. That could cause very serious concern to the Department of National Revenue, unless it did not issue the cheques.
There are other Clauses which concern me more than Clause 1. My colleagues and I will be speaking to them as they
March 11, 1983

would affect our constituents. The Committee of the Whole in the House of Commons is a very good forum in which to discuss legislation, presenting both sides of the argument. Once both sides of an argument have been presented on a certain Clause, I wish that we would move on. I am concerned about those two million people who have had their income tax returns processed and are waiting to receive their cheques. There will be millions more by the end of this month.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary or the Minister tell us what will happen if, by some chance-
The Bill doesn't pass.

-it does not pass? At which point will those taxpayers receive the refunds for which they are eligible? Is it completely contingent on the passing of Bill C-139? Will refunds be made to some two million people whose forms have already been processed and many millions more whose forms will be coming within the next couple of weeks?

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance has indicated that he is desirous of having this income tax Bill passed by the House, first, because it includes provisions which were first made public in 1981 and, second, because it includes subsequent amendments to the 1981 Bill or new initiatives of the Minister of Finance in the budget of June, 1982, or some of the resulting amendments introduced in the statement of the new Minister of Finance on October 27, 1982. He has urged this on the House in recognition of the fact that any income tax bill will have mixed effects, that it will affect different people differently. I assume the majority of Canadians represented by the Hon. Member for the Battlefords-Meadow Lake who has just spoken would benefit by the advantageous Clauses of this Bill. For example, they would benefit by the increase in the Child Tax Credit of $50 per child; by the reduction of the general rate to those in lower income levels, and by the new introduction of the $200 spousal allowance which, generally speaking, is of benefit to those of lower income levels. All of these would be available to those people when the Bill is passed.
Quite frankly, that is my personal motivation in seeing the House conclude consideration of this Bill as quickly as it can. Without having done a scientific analysis, I am convinced that of the many thousands of unemployed people in this country, many are the very people who will receive tax refunds. They are people who have paid taxes earlier in the year, who have then become unemployed, who are looking for some cash to assist them in a difficult time and who will be assisted by their refunds. That is why I support the Minister of Finance in doing as we have always done, having this legislation concluded before he introduces the next budget. That is my major motivation in urging the consideration and conclusion of this Bill as quickly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that and I would observe that if things continue as they have on Clause 1, it
Income Tax
could be past the end of April by the time we have Bill C-139 passed. I find it very disheartening that this amount of time would be taken, that the Chair, or whoever is responsible, allows the continuous and sometimes irrelevant interventions by some Members of this House on points that have already been covered in many instances.
If in fact those Members wish to continue to do that, what are the options that are open to the Government to see that the constituents of Canada get their income tax returns much sooner than would normally be the case if this kind of activity continues through the other Clauses of Bill C-139?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since this is in relation to House business and the Hon. Member asked for an opinion regarding how it can be made possible for this Bill to be adopted as early as possible in order to allow the refunds to be made, there is one simple Standing Order, namely No. 81, which would allow the Hon. Member's Party to agree with the Government to allocating a reasonable length of time, but a fixed length of time, to complete the debate.
If his Party is speaking in good faith, and I never doubted it, all he has to do is to ask his House Leader to come to an agreement on a reasonable period of time to conclude debate on the Bill. If the Hon. Member reads Standing Order 81, he will see that that option is available to him even if, as he deplores it, another Party in the House seems to be dragging its feet and filibustering this Bill at this time.

Mr. Chairman, following on that comment my question is that I would have trouble agreeing to that suggestion regarding the entire Bill because some sections could take up the whole amount of time that has been agreed to, and therefore some of the sections that we want to deal with would never in fact be dealt with in Committee of the Whole. My question would be, can this procedure that the Hon. Member has just outlined be used on a Clause by Clause basis?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Sorry, Mr. Chairman, I missed the last part of the question.
My question was, can this procedure that has been outlined be used on a Clause by Clause basis?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, unfortunately it cannot be done on a Clause by Clause basis because Standing Order 81 deals with stages of a Bill and not Clauses of a Bill. Standing Order 37 would be available to limit debate on specific Clauses, but I do not think that this would be appropriate.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to wrap up the debate on this particular amendment we have before the Committee. In my view the amendment has been explained pretty well. I just want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary one question. He will appreciate that in his example of the person who had a car which was rented for $300 a month and there was $100 in repairs, he came up with a 50 per cent tax cost and said that that would cost the employee $1,800 a year and that would be a pretty modest cost for a car. He will of course appreciate that this is a standby cost. It is not the employee's

March 11, 1983
Income Tax
car. It is a car that is owned by someone else for business purposes, because if the car was not a business car the company employing the employee could not deduct the car at all for business purposes. It has to be used in the business.
What we are talking about here, so the Parliamentary Secretary will understand, is that portion of the value in the vehicle and its repairs and so on that is attributable to the personal use of the car that can only be owned by the company if the car is a company car for business purposes, not for personal purposes.
I want to point out to him that if the employee has paid $7,200 for an automobile that he does not even own, it is probably not worth any more than a couple of thousand dollars at the end of a four-year period, that his own example has pointed out how horrendously unfair the 2 per cent standby charge is, and how horrendously unfair the percentage of maintenance cost is. If he would only look at it that way, let him take a look at the amendment we have proposed because our amendment is proposed on the basis of fairness.
I want to make it very clear that as far as we are concerned, employees should pay tax on the personal use of their cars owned by their employers, but that tax should be fair and should be fairly calculated. Two per cent is probably not bad, provided you calculate it on the value of the car. As the car gets older, the benefit gets smaller on the value of the car. That is probably fair that way. The Parliamentary Secretary will remember that we discussed this matter in the Standing Committee, and he will recall that the 2 per cent standby charge was before the Standing Committee, but the matter of charges for repairs or maintenance was not debated in the Standing Committee. He will know that it was only on the basis that the maintenance charges were not included and that the 2 per cent included the maintenance that the Standing Committee, of which he was a member, came to the conclusion that perhaps it was not all that bad. But you have added in the maintenance. So if you took the maintenance out, we could accept it the way it is. The problem is that the maintenance has been added in and the 2 per cent has been left in. In other words, the burden has been increased. That is what the objection to Clause 1 was all about in the first place.
Does the Parliamentary Secretary not realize that what we are looking for here is fairness? We are not trying to give anyone an advantage. We are trying to impress upon a Government, that will not think and will not move, what fairness is all about.
Before the Parliamentary Secretary gets up, he might also reflect on the fact that the Minister in his statement said that he saw $20 million in lost revenue because of this. He saw $80 million in lost revenue because of the annuity provision. He has lost all of the revenue there. He is not going to get any revenue, because of what he did yesterday. He got himself into employee benefits. He figured he would pick up some revenue because of employee benefits. I want to tell him that he probably lost revenue there with respect to professionals. What we want is an Income Tax Act that is fair, reasonable, honest and makes sense. The proposal here is to do that, to follow the
concepts that we discussed in the Standing Committee so that we can get a Bill before and out of this House, one that makes sense. That is the reason for the amendment. I would like the Minister's comment on that at this point. Then let us put that amendment because we would like to put another amendment with respect to maintenance costs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member should be reminded about a second question that arose in the Finance Committee, the question of complexity and the law, I would urge the Hon. Member to think about that principle before he begins to argue that the value of the car be a declining amount. Can he imagine the calculation that would be involved in such a process for an operation like Bell Canada? There would be an enormous amount of calculating that would have to go on long before the reporting of the individual could be made. I urge him to look at that.
Second, our officials tell me that reimbursable operating costs are already in the law and that the current section clarifies it because we have had some serious problems with reporting.
Third, I would suggest that he is probably right about my comments on repairs and $100 a month. I suspect that is overstated. I did it to round the figures out to a nice, even $3,600 a year. It looked like an easy calculation for me, but I think that is overstated. That is not what people will be smacked with in the early days of a car's operation. It may work out that, later on, the amount that is assigned would go up somewhat higher, but in the beginning of a car's life, I doubt that that would be the case. I also wonder whether an employer would keep a car around that would have heavy repair costs later in its life.
Finally, I would point out that the big question here is the question of whether it is fair or not fair to ask people to pay for personal use in after-tax dollars, and do we have an accurate amount. I would say yes in both cases. Mr. Chairman, with respect to Subclause 1(4) of the Bill, the effect is that the employee is required to pay tax on the maintenance cost of the vehicle. That maintenance cost, by all possible definitions, includes insurance that the employer would have to pay anyway. You cannot own a company car and not have it insured. The employee has to pay his share of the insurance just because he uses it personally.
The same applies to licences. If a company is going to own a car, it has to licence it. It could not be used for company business unless it was licensed. Therefore, there is no reason why an employee, directed by his employer to drive a company car, should have to pay a portion of the licence cost as a personal use item.
Indeed, there is no reason why the maintenance of the car in terms of grease, oil, tires and paint should be paid by the employee at all. After all, it is not his car. He cannot be given the car that he has used principally for enjoyment and only secondarily for business. It has to be a business car in order to be deductible. Therefore, what we are talking about is a business car.
The question really is whether it is fair that he should pay tax because the company decided to insure the car for SI million or $2 million. Is it fair that he should pay insurance on the basis that it was a business car and therefore subject to all sorts of additional insurance costs? He has to bear that in his personal tax because he may use it on the weekend part-time. Is it fair? I say it is not fair. If we are going to charge maintenance, we should do this. Therefore I move:

Mr. Chairman, I guess this afternoon is turning into an incredible experience. I was a new Member of this House in May of 1979, and Parliament met that fall. I guess when you are a newcomer you remember the initial legislation with which you were faced better than you may remember subsequent pieces, because they go by very rapidly sometimes. One of the first pieces of legislation the Clark Government had to bring before the House was the budget brought down in the fall of 1977 by the then Minister of Finance. If you follow the Minister's logic, you would have to conclude that there were no refund cheques sent out on the basis of the 1977 or 1978 tax years. We all know that is simply not true. The Clark Government was the Government which obeyed the law of Canada, and the law of Canada requires income tax refunds to be sent. There is a law, and if one is a Cabinet Minister and respects the law, one sends out refund cheques. If one chooses not to respect the law, there are many ways in which Parliament or Members of the Opposition can force Government Ministers to respect the law. We can implore them to do it. We can suggest they do it, but there is something particularly dishonourable and discredible when you have Ministers of the Crown standing in the House and telling Canadians that a law exists when in fact it does not exist.
I challenge the Cabinet Minister who spoke on the point of order or the Cabinet Minister responsible for this Bill to stand up in this House and tell us where in the law of Canada the Government is required not to send out refund cheques.
